'''Kathryn Rice Bullock'''  (September 24, 1945 – May 17, 2021)<ref name="ECS">{{cite web|title=Kathryn R. Bullock, ECS President, 1995-1996|url=http://www.electrochem.org/bullock|website=The Electrochemical Society|accessdate=21 June 2016}}</ref> was a chemist, best known for her work in developing  [[VRLA battery|valve-regulated lead-acid batteries]]. Her theoretical and statistical modeling of the [[electrochemistry]] of [[battery (electricity)|batteries]] led to better understanding of processes such as [[corrosion]] and advances in battery design.<ref name="BCI"/> Her work has applications for [[Hybrid vehicle|hybrid]] and [[electric car]]s, [[Home fuel cell|residential fuel cell systems]] and [[Thermal energy storage|solar energy storage]].<ref name="ECS"/><ref name="BCI"/><ref name="Batteries"/><ref name="Bullock2003">{{cite journal|last1=Bullock|first1=Kathryn R|title=Lead−acid battery research and development—a vital key to winning new business|journal=Journal of Power Sources|date=2003|volume=116|issue=1–2|pages=8–13|doi=10.1016/S0378-7753(02)00700-0|bibcode=2003JPS...116....8B|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/222615702|accessdate=21 June 2016}}</ref><ref name="Brodd">{{cite book|last1=Brodd|first1=Ralph J.|title=Batteries for sustainability selected entries from the Encyclopedia of Sustainability Science and Technology|date=2012|publisher=Springer|location=New York|isbn=978-1-4614-5791-6|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=iUH2Typ5d34C&pg=PA116}}</ref> Kathryn Bullock has published over 60 technical papers and holds at least 11 U.S. patents.<ref name="BCI"/>  She served as vice-president of the [[Electrochemical Society]] in 1992 and as president from 1995 to 1996.<ref name="ECS"/> Bullock died on May 17, 2021, from [[Alzheimer's disease]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://walkersfuneralservice.com/tribute-ajax/print-obituary.html?id=2897|title=Norma Kathryn Bullock|website=walkersfuneralservice}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
(Norma) Kathryn Rice (later Bullock)<ref name="World">{{cite book|title=The World Who's Who of Women 1992-93|chapter=BULLOCK, Norma Kathryn Rice|date=August 1, 1992|publisher=Taylor & Francis|volume=11|page=133}}</ref> was one of twins, born September 24, 1945, in [[Bartlesville, Oklahoma]], to Robert Bruce Rice and Norma Elaine Fanshier.<ref name="FANSHIER">{{cite web|title=Norma Elaine FANSHIER|url=http://familyharttng.info/getperson.php?personID=I590248&tree=FamilyHartTNG|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200210235747/http://familyharttng.info/getperson.php?personID=I590248&tree=FamilyHartTNG|url-status=dead|archive-date=February 10, 2020|website=The Family Hart Online Database|accessdate=21 June 2016}}</ref> Her twin sister Judith Rice (later Henderson) became a scholar of sixteenth-century literature. Their father, Robert B. Rice, was a geophysicist.<ref name="Batteries">{{cite web|title=Kathryn Bullock|url=http://www.batteriesinternational.com/kathryn-bullock/|website=Batteries International|date=March 1, 2015}}</ref><ref name="Bates">{{cite book|last1=Bates|first1=Charles C.|last2=Gaskell|first2=Thomas F.|last3=Rice|first3=Robert B.|title=Geophysics in the affairs of man.|date=1982|publisher=Pergamon Pr.|location=Oxford [usw.], Frankfurt|isbn=978-0080240251|page=492|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=B583BQAAQBAJ&pg=PA432|accessdate=21 June 2016}}</ref><ref name="SEG">{{cite web|title=Robert B. Rice|url=http://wiki.seg.org/wiki/Robert_B._Rice|website=SEG Wiki|accessdate=21 June 2016}}</ref> During summers Kathryn worked as a part-time secretary at Marathon Oil Company, where her father was employed. He encouraged her to pursue a scientific career.<ref name="Batteries"/>

Kathryn Rice attended the [[University of Colorado Boulder]], receiving a B.A. in English and a minor in chemistry in 1967.<ref name="ECS"/> She was the only female student in a lab of fifty men.   In 1967, Kathryn Rice married Kenneth Bullock, a seminary student.<ref name="Batteries"/>  They have two children, Kevin and Kerry.<ref name="Gaston"/>

Her first scientific position was as a combined secretary and technical staff person in a new battery development group, organized by John Devitt at [[Gates Corporation|Gates Rubber Company]] in [[Denver, Colorado]]. There Bullock became interested in nickel oxide-zinc [[Battery (electricity)|batteries]].<ref name="Batteries"/> She went to [[Northwestern University]] for further study, receiving an M.S. in chemistry in 1969 and a Ph.D. in physical chemistry in 1972.<ref name="ECS"/><ref name="Technology">{{cite book|chapter=Bullock, Kathryn R.|title=Who's who in Technology Today|date=1984|publisher=Technology Recognition Corporation|volume=3|page=189}}</ref> At Northwestern, she worked with Donald E. Smith, using alternating current [[polarography]] to study electrochemical reactions.<ref name="Batteries"/><ref name="Bullock1974">{{cite journal|last1=Bullock|first1=Kathryn R.|last2=Smith|first2=Donald E.|title=Fundamental and second harmonic alternating current polarography of electrode processes with coupled first-order preceding chemical reactions. Cadmium-nitrilotriacetate system|journal=Analytical Chemistry|date=July 1974|volume=46|issue=8|pages=1069–1074|doi=10.1021/ac60344a008}}</ref>

==Career==
In 1972, Bullock rejoined the Electrochemical Research Department of Gates Rubber Company. John Devitt's group at Gates was working on development of a [[VRLA battery|valve-regulated lead-acid battery]] (VRLA).<ref name="BCI">{{cite news|title=Battery Heroines: Kathryn Bullock - Faith, reason and a life in batteries|url=https://issuu.com/rizzo48/docs/bci_2015_lo|accessdate=23 June 2016|work=BCI 2015 Yearbook|agency=47-48|publisher=Batteries International|date=2015}}</ref> Prior to the development of VRLAs, "flooded" rechargeable lead-acid batteries were used.  They were filled with 30-40% sulfuric acid. At 85-90% of their charge capacity, chemical reactions within the battery became less effective, and water in the system was converted into hydrogen and oxygen gases.  Flooded batteries could not be sealed, and had to be monitored to ensure effectiveness and prevent problems. In contrast, VRLAs were designed to ensure that oxygen would recombine rather than being lost. VRLAs contain acid inside a silica gel or absorb it into a porous glass separator. Gases that do not recombine are vented through a one-way pressure-release valve.<ref name="Siddesh"/>  Bullock developed computer models describing the relationships between the circuit voltage of VRLAs and their acid concentration, battery charge and internal temperature.<ref name="ECS"/><ref name="BCI"/><ref name="Batteries"/> She read widely and was inspired by the work of people like [[Jeanne Burbank]], Paul Ruetschi, and [[Detchko Pavlov]].<ref name="Batteries"/> She studied corrosion within batteries. She examined the effects of adding [[phosphoric acid]] to lead dioxide electrodes in gel batteries to increase battery cycle life, resulting in the creation of batteries with low levels of phosphoric acid. In 1977, Bullock joined Globe-Union, Inc. in Milwaukee, where she continued her work with VRLAs.<ref name="ECS"/><ref name="BCI"/><ref name="Batteries"/>  Her work on the effects of adding [[phosphoric acid]] to lead dioxide electrodes won her the Battery Division Research Award from the Electrochemical Society in 1980.<ref name="ECS"/><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Bullock|first1=Kathryn R.|title=The Effect of Phosphoric Acid on the Positive Electrode in the Lead Acid Battery|journal=Journal of the Electrochemical Society|date=1977|volume=124|issue=10|pages=1478–1482|doi=10.1149/1.2133095|doi-access=free|bibcode=1977JElS..124.1478B }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Bullock|first1=Kathryn R.|title=The Effect of Phosphoric Acid on the Positive Electrode in the Lead-Acid Battery|journal=Journal of the Electrochemical Society|date=1979|volume=126|issue=3|pages=360|doi=10.1149/1.2129044}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Bullock|first1=Kathryn R.|title=The Effect of Phosphoric Acid on the Positive Electrode in the Lead-Acid Battery|journal=Journal of the Electrochemical Society|date=1979|volume=126|issue=11|pages=1848|doi=10.1149/1.2128813|doi-access=free}}</ref>

In 1980, Bullock became manager of Globe-Union's Chemical Research Department, which later became part of Johnson Controls, Inc. At Johnson, funded in part by the [[U.S. Department of Energy]], she and William Tiedemann developed JCI's Battery Technology Center. They did early research in areas including [[Thermal management (electronics)|thermal management]], grid corrosion, grid design, and load leveling, developing many different types of batteries including [[Electric vehicle battery|electric vehicle batteries]]. Bullock filed a number of patents on methods for improving battery design, production and performance.<ref name="BCI"/>

In 1991, she was invited to lead a battery development group at [[AT&T Bell Labs]] (later [[Lucent]]). Her work on the development of batteries has led to improved designs which have been licensed and used all over the world.<ref name="ECS"/><ref name="BCI"/><ref name="Batteries"/><ref name="Siddesh">{{cite book|last1=Siddesh|first1=Gaddadevara Matt|last2=Deka|first2=Ganesh Chandra|last3=Srinivasa|first3=Krishnarajanagar GopalaIyengar|last4=Patnaik|first4=Lalit Mohan|title=Cyber-Physical Systems: A Computational Perspective|date=2015|publisher=Chapman and Hall|location=Boca Raton, Florida|pages=200–202|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hpDwCgAAQBAJ&pg=PA200|accessdate=21 June 2016|isbn=9781482259773}}</ref><ref name="Bullock1994">{{cite journal|last1=Bullock|first1=K. R.|title=Lead/acid batteries|journal=Journal of Power Sources|date=1994|volume=51|issue=1|pages=1–17|doi=10.1016/0378-7753(94)01952-5|bibcode=1994JPS....51....1B|s2cid=105192302 }}</ref> With AT&T Bell Labs's Power Systems Business Unit, she received the [[Deming Prize]] of the [[Japanese Union of Scientists and Engineers]] in 1994.<ref name="Kushnir"/><ref name="Donnell"/>

In 1996, AT&T Bell Labs became Lucent Technologies, and Bullock joined [[Medtronic, Inc.]] to develop lithium batteries for use in medical devices.<ref name="ECS"/> She remained there for three years before becoming vice-president of C&D Technologies, Inc., where she remained for another three years. In 2003, she formed Coolohm, Inc., a consulting company specializing in power sources. She studied the role of carbon in battery design,<ref name="BCI"/> and taught classes in power sources as an adjunct faculty member at [[Villanova University]].<ref name="NASBio">{{cite web|title=Review of the U.S. DRIVE Research Program, Phase 4|url=http://www8.nationalacademies.org/cp/committeeview.aspx?key=49373|website=The National Academies|accessdate=23 June 2016}}</ref> She served on a number of policy-related committees and projects.<ref name="Effectiveness">{{cite book|last1=Committee to Review the U.S. Advanced Battery Consortium's Electric Vehicle Battery Research and Development Project Selection Process; Commission on Engineering and Technical Systems; National Research Council|title=Effectiveness of the United States Advanced Battery Consortium as a government-industry partnership|date=1998|publisher=National Academy Press|location=Washington, D.C.|isbn=978-0-309-06143-8|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=i8tTAgAAQBAJ&pg=PR3|accessdate=23 June 2016}}</ref><ref name="Review">{{cite book|last1=Committee on Review of the U.S. DRIVE Research Program, Phase 4, Board on Energy and Environmental Systems, Division on Engineering and Physical Sciences, National Research Council of the National Academies|title=Review of the Research Program of the U.S. DRIVE Partnership : fourth report|date=2013|publisher=National Academies Press|location=Washington, D.C.|isbn=978-0-309-26831-8|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=oxF1AgAAQBAJ&pg=PA158|accessdate=23 June 2016}}</ref>

Bullock was an active member of the [[Electrochemical Society]], which she 
joined in 1972. She helped to organize the Rocky Mountain (1973) and Southern Wisconsin (1982) Sections. She held a variety of appointments on offices and committees, most importantly as vice-president of the society in 1992 and as president from 1995 to 1996.<ref name="ECS"/>

==Awards and honors==
Bullock has received a number of awards and honors including the following: 
* [[Gaston Planté]] Medalist from the [[Bulgarian Academy of Sciences]] (1996)<ref name="Gaston">{{cite journal|last1=Bullock|first1=K.R.|title=The 1996 Gaston Planté Medal acceptance speech|journal=Journal of Power Sources|date=January 1997|volume=64|issue=1–2|pages=9–10|doi=10.1016/S0378-7753(97)83326-5|bibcode=1997JPS....64....9B|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/238168372|accessdate=21 June 2016|doi-access=free}}</ref>
* [[Deming Prize]] of the [[Japanese Union of Scientists and Engineers]], as part of the [[AT&T Bell Labs]]/[[Lucent Technologies]] Power  Systems  unit (1994)<ref name="Kushnir">{{cite web|last1=Kushnir|first1=Anna|title=Deming Prize|url=http://www.freequality.org/documents/knowledge/deming%20prize.pdf|website=Free Quality|accessdate=21 June 2016|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304194923/http://www.freequality.org/documents/knowledge/deming%20prize.pdf|archivedate=4 March 2016}}</ref><ref name="Donnell">{{cite book|last1=Donnell|first1=A. J.|title=Nineteenth IEEE: CPMT International Electronics Manufacturing Technology Symposium, October 14-16, 1996, Austin, TX, USA|date=1996|publisher=Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers|location=New York|isbn=978-0-7803-3642-1|pages=416–421|chapter=SPC implementation for improving product quality|doi=10.1109/IEMT.1996.559778|s2cid=110748846 }}</ref>
* [[Fellow of the Royal Society of Chemistry]] (1988)<ref name="ECS"/>
* Fellow of the [[American Institute of Chemists]] (1987)<ref name="ECS"/>
* [[Electrochemical Society|ECS]] Battery Division Research Award (1980)<ref name="ECS"/>
* Electrochemical Society Summer fellow (1969)<ref name="ECS"/>
* [[National Institutes of Health]] Fellow (1972)<ref name="ECS"/>
* [[Phi Beta Kappa Society]] (1966)<ref name="ECS"/>
